scenes.title: 1998 Pittsburgh Partition Table: Twin Paintbrushes Stroking Hidden Real Hand & Visible Rubber Hand in Sync
scenes.era: 1998, University of Pittsburgh / Carnegie Mellon cognitive neuroscience lab

layout.description: Sunlit psychology laboratory table divided by a crisp vertical matte-white wooden partition screen: behind the screen rests the 45-year-old participant's real left hand (visible to our camera, hidden from the participant); in plain view before their chest sits a realistic prosthetic left hand above an under-table millimeter drift ruler.

positions.who: Pittsburgh experimenter (2.5D matte cream-white vinyl researcher in crisp white lab coat and collared shirt)
positions.where: seated across the table holding two identical camel-hair paintbrushes and stroking the visible rubber index knuckle and hidden real index knuckle in exact unison

positions.who: 45-year-old volunteer (2.5D matte cream-white vinyl adult in rolled-sleeve burgundy knit sweater)
positions.where: watching the visible prosthetic hand intently as brushstrokes land in sync, then sliding their right index finger under the table 23 mm toward the rubber hand
positions.facing: seated facing tabletop partition and rubber hand

props.name: vertical tabletop occlusion partition and realistic prosthetic left hand
props.period_detail: hides the volunteer's real left hand from sight while aligning the prosthetic hand naturally with the left shoulder
props.physical_behavior: State-A lifeless detached rubber prop on desk -> State-B volunteer's hidden real hand jerking back protectively whenever a reflex hammer nears the rubber fingers

props.name: matched pair of camel-hair paintbrushes and under-table millimeter ruler
props.period_detail: delivers synchronous vs 500 ms asynchronous brush strokes and records the 23 mm pointing shift
props.physical_behavior: State-A twin brushes poised above knuckles -> State-B sweeping down simultaneously across rubber and real fingers in rhythmic unison

actions.verb_sequence: strokes hidden real hand and visible rubber hand in crisp unison for 60 seconds -> guides blindfolded volunteer to point underneath the tabletop ruler
closes eyes and slides right index finger under the table -> lands 23 mm shifted toward the rubber hand -> opens eyes in stunned disbelief

reactions.reaction: wide-eyed astonishment staring from the millimeter ruler up to the lifeless rubber glove
calm nod contrasting 23 mm synced shift against 13 mm unsynced control

scenes.wardrobe: Late-1990s university attire: crisp white lab coat over light-blue button-down shirt; adult volunteer in burgundy crew-neck knit sweater.
scenes.lighting: Clean high-key studio window daylight illuminating both sides of the tabletop partition.
scenes.recognition_hook: Hide your real hand behind a board, brush a lifeless rubber hand in sync for sixty seconds, and your brain relocates where your own fingers live by 23 millimeters!

key_visual.description: a psychology table divided by a vertical partition where an experimenter uses two matching paintbrushes to stroke an adult participant's hidden real hand and a visible prosthetic hand in unison above a millimeter drift ruler

scenes.title: 2005 Control Test: Out-of-Sync Brushing & Wooden Block Breaking the Ownership Spell

layout.description: Bright testing desk where the experimenter alternates brush strokes half a second out of sync and swaps the rubber hand for a plain rectangular wooden block.

positions.where: watching alternating left-then-right brushstrokes and a plain rectangular wood block produce zero illusion

props.name: rectangular wooden block control and alternating paintbrushes
props.period_detail: proves both millisecond synchrony and human hand geometry are required (Tsakiris & Haggard 2005)
props.physical_behavior: State-A synced rubber hand (illusion ON) -> State-B swapped for plain wood block with 500 ms delayed strokes (volunteer shakes head NO)

actions.verb_sequence: delays second brush by 500 milliseconds and places wooden block -> volunteer points accurately straight to real hidden hand

reactions.reaction: calm, unfooled head shake as body-map check rejects the block

scenes.wardrobe: Smart-casual collared shirt and lab coat.
scenes.recognition_hook: Delay one paintbrush by half a second — or swap the rubber hand for a block of wood — and your premotor security check kills the illusion cold.

scenes.title: Sunlit Outdoor Tennis & Garden Courtyard: Everyday Adult Tool Embodiment in Action
scenes.era: Modern sunlit outdoor neighborhood tennis court & garden walkway

layout.description: Open-air sunlit neighborhood court and garden patio where a 50-year-old adult effortlessly bounces a tennis ball on the center strings of a racket without looking down, experiencing synchronized visual-plus-tactile handle feedback.

positions.who: 50-year-old adult player (in crisp white polo shirt and navy shorts)
positions.where: standing in open morning sunlight bouncing a yellow tennis ball rhythmically off the racket face as an extension of their own palm

props.name: strung tennis racket and bright yellow ball in open sunlight
props.period_detail: illustrates everyday premotor-parietal body-schema extension through synced sight and handle vibration
props.physical_behavior: State-A racket held loose at side -> State-B crisp rhythmic ball bounce on strings in effortless hand-eye-touch lock

actions.verb_sequence: raises racket into morning sunlight -> bounces ball cleanly off sweet spot three times while chatting effortlessly

reactions.reaction: confident, natural poise as the brain treats the tool tip like living fingertips

scenes.wardrobe: Crisp white athletic polo, navy shorts, court shoes.
scenes.lighting: Bright golden outdoor morning sunlight across green court and trees.
scenes.recognition_hook: The exact 60-second rule that tricked volunteers into owning rubber is how your brain turns a car bumper, chef's knife, or tennis racket into part of your own arm!
